title: How much is it?
goal: Ask prices, give your age and phone number — and for that, fit in two things English doesn't do: numbers that agree in gender, and plural nouns that change their whole ending.
bekal: count from 0 to 100, including knowing when to slip in the little word *de*
form the plural of masculine, feminine, and neuter nouns — with the three most common sound changes
ask and answer about prices, age, and phone numbers

dialogs.title: Dialogue — La chioșc
dialogs.intro: Budi and Ioana stop at a ticket kiosk near the bus stop. Budi needs a bus ticket; while they wait, Ioana realizes she doesn't have Budi's phone number yet.

notes: **Cât costă?** The verb is *a costa*, and *costă* works for one item or several: *Cât costă un bilet?* and *Cât costă biletele?* In the *-a* verb group, the "he/she" and "they" forms are always twins. One form for every price — a small gift from this language.

**Cinci lei, but optzeci *de* lei.** From 20 up, Romanian slips *de* between the number and the noun; literally "eighty of lei". Below 20 there's nothing: *zece lei*, *nouăsprezece lei*. This is the mistake that lasts longest for learners, so build the habit now.

**Am douăzeci și opt de ani.** Age is something you **have**, not something you "are": the verb is *a avea* from unit 3, just like French or Spanish. The question is *Câți ani ai?* — "how many years do you have?". *Câți* is the masculine plural form because *an* is masculine; for feminine and neuter nouns use *câte*: *Câte bilete?*

**Doi frați, două surori, două bilete.** The number two agrees with the gender of its noun. The surprise: *bilet* is neuter, and neuter nouns behave as feminine in the plural — so *două bilete*, not *doi bilete*. That's what "masculine in the singular, feminine in the plural" from unit 3 means in real life.

**Prea scump** = too expensive; don't confuse it with *foarte scump* (very expensive). And notice the order in *numărul tău de telefon*: the possessive sticks right onto the noun with its article, and only then comes *de telefon*.

grammars.title: Numbers 0–100
body: Romanian numbers are cousins of the Latin numbers you already know from English words: *doi* (duo), *trei* (trio), *opt* (octave), *zece* (decimal). The pattern is regular: teens = unit + *-sprezece* ("over ten"), tens = unit + *-zeci* ("tens").
Watch out for three shortened forms: **pai**sprezece (14), **șai**sprezece (16), and **șai**zeci (60) — not *patrusprezece*, *șasesprezece*, *șasezeci*.

head: Number
Română
Say it
rows: *douăzeci și unu · treizeci și cinci · nouăzeci și nouă*

after: **Unu, un, o.** For counting, phone numbers, and at the end of compound numbers, use *unu*: *zero, unu, doi…*, *douăzeci și unu*. But in front of a noun, "one" is nothing other than the indefinite article you already know: *un bilet*, *o cafea*. Never say *unu bilet*.
**Doi and două spread into compound numbers:** *doisprezece lei* but *douăsprezece bilete*; *douăzeci și doi de ani* but *douăzeci și două de cafele*. The other numbers don't care about gender.

**The *de* rule:** 1–19 go straight to the noun (*cinci lei, nouăsprezece ani*), 20–100 use *de* (*douăzeci de lei, optzeci și cinci de ani, o sută de lei*). If the noun isn't mentioned, *de* disappears too: *Câți ani ai? — Douăzeci și opt.*
On the street you'll hear clipped teens: *unșpe, doișpe, treișpe, paișpe, cinșpe, șaișpe…* That's everyday speech; just recognize it for now, no need to copy it.

grammars.title: Noun plurals
body: English mostly just adds *-s*. Romanian changes the whole ending, and which ending depends on the noun's gender.

head: Gender
Plural ending
Singular → plural
rows: *student → studenți, frate → frați, leu → lei, an → ani*

after: **The *-i* ending softens the letter before it.** These three changes come up all the time: **t → ț** (*student → studenți, frate → frați*), **d → z** (*stradă → străzi*), **s → ș** (*urs → urși*, bear). Remember from the Pronunciation chapter: the *-i* itself is barely heard — *studenți* is read stoo-DEHNTS'.

**Vowels in the middle of the word often shift too:** *a → e* (*fată → fete*), *a → ă* (*stradă → străzi, carte → cărți*), *o → oa* (*telefon → telefoane*). Some are truly irregular — like English *man → men*: *soră → surori*, *om → oameni* (person), *copil → copii* (child).

Honestly: for feminine and neuter nouns, no rule always predicts *-e* or *-i*, *-uri* or *-e*. Romanians themselves learn them word by word. That's why from this unit on the vocabulary list gives the plural — *bilet, bilete* — so learn the two as a pair.

head: At the checkout
English
rows: Do you have small change? / I don't have small change.

blocks.title: Romanian money
items: The currency is the **leu** (code RON), plural **lei**. *Leu* also means "lion" — so technically you pay for your coffee with a few lions.
The banknotes aren't paper: they're all **polymer** (plastic), waterproof and hard to tear. They come in 1, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100, 200, and 500 lei. The coins are 1, 5, 10, and 50 bani.

Cards are accepted almost everywhere in București, but at markets, small kiosks, and in villages cash is still king. Prices in this book are just examples for practicing numbers; real prices change all the time.

head: Sentence
English
rows: *Câți ani are Andrei? — Are douăzeci și doi de ani.*
How old is Andrei? — He's twenty-two.

blocks.text: Look at the fourth row: *nouăsprezece ani* without *de*, because nineteen is still under twenty — while *douăzeci și doi **de** ani* uses it. Age is the best place to practice this rule, since you'll be asked your age far more often than you think. Asking someone's age is normal among peers in Romania; with older people or people you've just met, wait for them to raise the topic.

blocks.title: How Romanians give phone numbers
items: Romanian mobile numbers have ten digits and always start with **07**. The country code is **+40**; when you use it, drop the leading zero.
Numbers are usually dictated digit by digit in groups of three or four, just like Budi does. Some people read them in pairs — *zero șapte, douăzeci și doi…* — so your tens need to be ready.
The numbers 1 and 2 in phone numbers are always masculine: *unu, doi* — not *una, două*.
